title: If you find anything better
hook: if you find anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, turn to it; if not, make room for nothing else (Meditations 3.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was answer openly. Your line was could I say it: think only what you could say out loud.

Most advice tells you what to want. Marcus Aurelius does something stranger: he issues a challenge, aimed at himself. Go ahead, he says. Search all of human life. If you find something better than these four things, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy it. He isn't defending a position. He's daring himself to beat it. An emperor who could have anything, asking what's actually worth having. Today: if you find anything better.
screen: `A CHALLENGE, AIMED AT HIMSELF.` → `SEARCH ALL OF HUMAN LIFE.` → `IF YOU FIND ANYTHING BETTER.`

segments.voice: The four are justice, truth, self-control and courage. Readers of Plato will hear the old Greek list of four virtues, where wisdom usually stands. Marcus puts truth in that place, which tells you something about him: for a man surrounded by flatterers, truth was a daily discipline. Then the dare. If you find anything better than these, turn to it. He raises the stakes: if you find anything better than the guiding spirit inside you, the reason that governs your choices and keeps you honest, take that instead. And he answers himself. If nothing better turns up, and he expects nothing will, make room for nothing else. Next come the rivals that usually crowd in: praise from the crowd, power, wealth, the enjoyment of pleasures. He doesn't call them evil. His worry is subtler. Let one sit beside the four as an equal, even briefly, and it starts to take over without asking. A second loyalty quietly becomes the first. So, he writes, simply and freely choose the better, and hold on to it. Not a long calculation every morning, weighing virtue against convenience. One plain choice, then kept. And it gives any day four questions. Was I fair? Was I true? Did I hold back where I needed to? Did I do the hard thing? The dare stays open.
screen: `THE FOUR: JUSTICE, TRUTH, CONTROL, COURAGE.` · `THE DARE: FIND SOMETHING BETTER.` · `THE RIVALS: PRAISE, POWER, WEALTH.` · `CHOOSE SIMPLY, AND HOLD ON.` · then, large: `NOTHING BETTER.`

segments.voice: Walk back through your day so far, or yesterday if it's early, and find one moment for each of the four: being fair, being true, holding back, doing the uncomfortable thing. Don't grade too hard. Just notice which got the most room, and which got crowded out.
Self-control. One of the four goods in Marcus's dare, alongside justice, truth and courage: if you find anything better, turn to it. If not, give room to nothing else. Today's word.
Your line: nothing better. One plain choice, made simply, then kept. Day five hundred forty-two, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the four virtues of Meditations 3.6 as an evening check: was I just, truthful, self-controlled and brave today?

myth: Marcus forbids looking for anything better than the four
he dares himself to look: if you find something better, he says, turn to it.
Marcus worries that rivals like praise slowly take over
let one sit beside the four as an equal, and it starts to take the lead.
Marcus calls wealth and pleasure evil in this passage
his worry is that they compete with the good, not that they are evil.

options: take it: money is a kind of good too.

fork.reveal: Marcus asks whether anything is better than justice and truth; if not, it gets no room beside them.

original.note: Greek, 'sound-mindedness': self-control, one of the four goods Marcus names in 3.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of virtues to admire.
what it means: a dare. find anything better and take it; if you can't, let nothing compete.
what a scholar hears: the four echo the Greek cardinal virtues, but Marcus sets truth where Plato's list has wisdom.

being harsh with yourself whenever you make a mistake

chat.says: What did Marcus think was worth more than praise or money?
options: Justice, truth, self-control and courage; if nothing beats them, nothing else gets room.
Fame that lasts after death, since it outlives any amount of money or praise.
Power, because with enough of it you can protect justice and truth for others.
chat.meaning: Marcus names justice, truth, self-control and courage, and dares himself to find anything better. If nothing beats them, nothing else gets room.

Plato.meaning: Athenian philosopher whose four virtues include wisdom

Marcus Aurelius.meaning: Roman emperor and Stoic who wrote notes to himself

guiding spirit.meaning: Marcus's inner reason that governs choices and keeps you honest

notes: 3.6: the four are given in the Greek as justice, truth, temperance (sophrosyne) and courage; Long renders 'justice, truth, temperance, fortitude'. Confirm.
3.6 names the rivals as praise from the many, power, wealth and enjoyment of pleasures, and warns they can 'suddenly' prevail; confirm paraphrase.
'Simply and freely choose the better, and hold to it' paraphrases Long's 3.6; confirm.
Plato's Republic 4 lists wisdom, courage, temperance and justice; the claim that Marcus puts truth where wisdom usually stands is an interpretive observation: confirm it is fair.

3.6 names the daimon, the 'deity planted in thee' (Long), as the second thing to beat; rendered as 'the guiding spirit inside you, the reason that governs your choices', matching day 541's 'spirit within'. Confirm.
